3. python scripts/build-html.py   -- regenerates the DATA_START..DATA_END block in the HTML
_meta.presentation: Defender and leadership briefing; evidence-first presentation, 2026-09-15

threats.title: Prompt Injection
threats.wild: 4/5 — provider-confirmed field AI-wrapper key theft; EchoLeak individually 3/5
threats.desc: Manipulation of LLM behavior through crafted inputs that override system-level instructions. Attack surface extends to any content the model parses — not just text input fields.
subtypes: Direct PI — user input explicitly overrides system prompt
Indirect PI — adversarial content in RAG/documents/search results
Multi-turn PI — injection spread across conversation turns
Cross-context PI — propagates between agents
Purchased PI Template — pre-optimized jailbreak from underground market
T01-SESSION — Session contamination, goal hijacking, and incremental escalation across a trajectory
threats.surface: Text input, RAG pipeline, document ingestion, API messages field, tool outputs
threats.update: v1.5: Standard per-event detectors fail against slow-burn multi-turn attacks. Temporal accumulation detection required. v1.9: T01-SESSION — Session contamination, goal hijacking, and incremental escalation across a trajectory
threats.applies_when: Untrusted emails, documents or web pages are treated as instructions.
threats.business_impact: Sensitive data may be disclosed or an authorized workflow redirected.
threats.defender_action: Restrict data access and outbound destinations; authorize actions outside the model. Test answers and remote-image requests as well as tools.
threats.evidence_summary: Field incidents support this category. EchoLeak was a production-system demonstration, with no customer impact reported by its discoverer.

threats.title: Excessive Agency
threats.wild: 4/5 — provider-confirmed field AI-wrapper key theft; EchoLeak individually 3/5
threats.desc: Excess permissions amplify prompt injection into unauthorised actions. Sensitive context can also leave through answers, read-only queries or renderer requests without model write tools.
subtypes: Unbounded tool access — model calls any registered tool without confirmation
Privilege escalation via PI
Chained tool use — multi-step chain without human review
Cross-system action — email, file write, payment outside AI boundary
threats.surface: Tool registration, function calling API, MCP servers
threats.plain_title: The assistant has more access than it needs
threats.applies_when: The assistant can read, send, change or execute beyond the user’s intended task.
threats.business_impact: A manipulated assistant can turn a small mistake into a data leak or unauthorized transaction.
threats.defender_action: Use per-user permissions and narrow tool access. Bind approvals to the exact recipient, data and action.
threats.evidence_summary: Field key theft supports this risk. The impact depends on the actual permissions and reachable data.

threats.title: Supply Chain Compromise
threats.wild: 4/5 — JFrog/ReversingLabs confirmed malicious models on HuggingFace
threats.desc: Compromised models, adapters, dependencies, servers or skills can execute malicious code or alter behavior. Normal-looking answers do not establish safety.
subtypes: Malicious model on public registry
Backdoored LoRA/PEFT adapter
Compromised MCP server or skill package
Poisoned dependency (pip/npm)
T03-SKILL — Skill lifecycle compromise across admission, retrieval, planner selection, execution, and updates
threats.surface: Model registry, adapter repository, dependency install, MCP marketplace
threats.update: v1.9: T03-SKILL — Skill lifecycle compromise across admission, retrieval, planner selection, execution, and updates September: T03-SKILL 4/5 for observed malicious distribution; include mutable dependencies, startup code and persistence.
threats.plain_title: A component you install is compromised
threats.applies_when: Models, skills, adapters or software dependencies come from a compromised supplier or distribution path.
threats.business_impact: Installed code may steal credentials or compromise the systems running the assistant.
threats.defender_action: Inventory and pin components, verify provenance, isolate execution and restrict secrets. A valid signature does not prove the component is safe.
threats.evidence_summary: Malicious model and skill distribution is documented. This does not establish that every behavioral-backdoor or skill-selection technique has field victims.

threats.title: Data / Model Poisoning
threats.wild: 3/5 — mixed subtype evidence; training research and retrieval injection are distinct
threats.desc: Training, fine-tuning, feedback or RAG facts can be tampered with. A model can faithfully repeat poisoned facts without following an injected instruction.
subtypes: Training data poisoning — corrupted data influences model weights
Fine-tuning dataset poisoning
RAG context poisoning — injecting adversarial documents at index time
Feedback loop poisoning — RLHF reward hacking via manipulated ratings
Factual RAG poisoning without instruction override — DATA-DEF-1
threats.surface: Training pipeline, fine-tuning datasets, RAG document stores, feedback/rating systems
threats.plain_title: Poisoned data changes answers or behavior
threats.applies_when: An attacker can influence retrieved documents, training data or fine-tuning datasets.
threats.business_impact: Decisions can be biased, answers corrupted or later behavior redirected.
threats.defender_action: Apply DATA-DEF-1: authorize data changes, corroborate consequential facts, track dataset versions and test derived-data/model rollback.
threats.evidence_summary: Evidence differs by subtype: training/fine-tuning attacks are heavily research-based; poisoned retrieval overlaps with prompt injection. The category score is 3/5 in the taxonomy.

threats.title: System Prompt Leakage
threats.wild: 3/5 — Extraction techniques documented; iterative prompting required
threats.desc: Extraction of system prompts, API keys, or proprietary instructions through iterative prompting or context manipulation.
subtypes: Direct extraction — asking the model to repeat its system prompt
Indirect extraction — inferring instructions from model behavior
API key/secret leakage embedded in system prompt
T05-CAPABILITY — Capability and architecture disclosure that enables a separately scored follow-on attack
threats.surface: System prompt, developer message, any context containing secrets
threats.update: v1.9: T05-CAPABILITY — Capability and architecture disclosure that enables a separately scored follow-on attack
threats.plain_title: Hidden instructions or secrets are disclosed
threats.applies_when: Internal prompts, credentials or sensitive architecture details enter model context.
threats.business_impact: Secrets can leak; disclosed tool or approval details may help a follow-on attack.
threats.defender_action: Keep credentials out of prompts. Enforce authorization in the application and assess what a disclosure would actually enable.
threats.evidence_summary: Extraction techniques are documented. Revealing ordinary prompt wording is not automatically a serious breach.

threats.title: Model Extraction
threats.desc: Query-based replication of proprietary models. Low risk for general-purpose LLMs; elevated for specialized or fine-tuned models with significant IP.
subtypes: Black-box extraction via crafted query sequences
Distillation from API outputs
threats.surface: Public API endpoints with high query volume access
threats.plain_title: Queries help copy a proprietary model
threats.applies_when: A valuable specialized model exposes enough query access to an attacker.
threats.business_impact: The organization may lose some value in proprietary model behavior or training investment.
threats.defender_action: Assess the model’s business value, restrict abusive query volume and monitor extraction patterns.
threats.evidence_summary: Research demonstrations support the technique; the corpus does not establish widespread theft of general-purpose frontier models by this route.

threats.title: Embedding / Vector Weaknesses
threats.wild: 2/5 — Specialized techniques; requires large query volume
threats.desc: Reconstructing sensitive information from embedding vectors, or leaking data through query-pattern side channels in vector stores.
subtypes: Embedding inversion — reconstructing training data from embedding vectors
Cross-tenant vector store leakage
Query-pattern side channel — inferring other users' data from search patterns
threats.surface: Embedding APIs, vector stores/databases, similarity search endpoints
threats.applies_when: Sensitive information is stored in vectors or shared retrieval infrastructure.
threats.business_impact: Private records may be reconstructed or returned to the wrong tenant.
threats.defender_action: Enforce tenant separation and retrieval authorization. Test what information vectors and search responses disclose.
threats.evidence_summary: Specialized extraction techniques are research-based. Cross-tenant access failures are a separate boundary to test; the aggregate score does not prove every subtype has occurred.

threats.title: Denial of Service / Unbounded Consumption
threats.desc: Context/quota exhaustion degrading LLM service availability. Enterprise metered APIs can be financially destructive — attacker pays nothing, victim loses service AND pays for the calls.
subtypes: Context window exhaustion — max-length inputs
API quota exhaustion — standard API (score 12)
Enterprise metered API exhaustion — $10K+/month budgets (score 16)
Rate limit abuse
threats.surface: Any LLM API endpoint; metered enterprise deployments especially
threats.plain_title: Requests exhaust the service or its budget
threats.applies_when: A public or shared assistant consumes metered inference, context or retry capacity.
threats.business_impact: Users lose service and the organization can incur unexpected usage costs.
threats.defender_action: Enforce per-user and aggregate request, token, concurrency, retry and spend ceilings. Test the cutoff; a cost alert is not a spending limit.
threats.evidence_summary: The framework rates resource exhaustion 4/5. This is an established service-abuse pattern; its business impact depends on quotas, billing and enforced limits.

threats.title: Multi-Agent Context Propagation
threats.wild: 3/5 — Source-confirmed data-flow risk; exploitation depends on deployment
threats.desc: PI propagates between chained agents, amplifying impact. Each agent hop can escalate privilege. Common in enterprise RAG and agentic assistant deployments.
subtypes: Output-to-input propagation
Privilege escalation across agent chain
MCP / A2A protocol injection
Agent-to-agent trust exploitation
Slow-Burn / Temporal Accumulation PI — distributed across multi-turn trajectory, below per-event threshold
T09-MEMORY — Persistent cross-session memory poisoning
T09-IDENTITY — Inter-agent identity, delegation, and privilege escalation
threats.surface: Multi-agent pipelines, MCP servers, A2A communication, LangChain/AutoGen deployments
threats.update: Source: LangGraph ToolNode.invoke() returns unsanitized ToolMessage to shared messages state — structurally confirmed Jun 2026. MA-DEF-1 effectiveness is MEDIUM in default LangGraph; requires explicit ToolCallWrapper enforcement for HIGH. v1.9: T09-MEMORY — Persistent cross-session memory poisoning; T09-IDENTITY — Inter-agent identity, delegation, and privilege escalation September: T09-MEMORY 3/5 overall; InjecMEM controlled method 2/5. Include normal-input ingestion, shared artifacts and version-aware MCP authorization.
threats.plain_title: One agent passes poisoned instructions to another
threats.applies_when: Agents share messages, summaries, memory or artifact stores across different permission levels.
threats.business_impact: Untrusted content may reach a more privileged worker and trigger an unauthorized action.
threats.defender_action: Authenticate delegation, isolate shared state and re-authorize at execution. A tool-free intermediary does not stop the chain.
threats.evidence_summary: 3/5 reflects demonstrated or source-confirmed paths, not a confirmed widespread multi-agent attack campaign. Memory demonstrations are 3/5; the specific InjecMEM study is 2/5.

threats.title: Non-Text Injection
threats.desc: Image, audio, or structured data injection bypassing text-focused input filters. Impact 4 because it circumvents most standard detection.
subtypes: Image-embedded PI (vision models)
Audio injection via ASR pipeline
Structured data (JSON/XML/CSV) injection
PDF/document visual injection
T10-CUA — Computer-use visual-state disagreement and deceptive UI actions
T10-REPRESENTATION — Representation confusion (monitored; pipeline-specific evidence required)
threats.surface: Multi-modal endpoints, vision models, ASR pipelines, document ingestion
threats.update: v1.9: T10-CUA — Computer-use visual-state disagreement and deceptive UI actions; T10-REPRESENTATION — Representation confusion (monitored; pipeline-specific evidence required)
threats.plain_title: Instructions arrive through images or other formats
threats.applies_when: The assistant interprets images, audio, documents, structured data or computer interfaces.
threats.business_impact: A deceptive input may influence answers or cause an incorrect interface action.
threats.defender_action: Test each supported format and verify the final action and destination. Text-only screening does not cover every input channel.
threats.evidence_summary: The category is research-backed at 2/5. Representation confusion remains a 1/5 monitored subtype; reproduce it in the actual conversion pipeline.

threats.title: Output Validation Failures
threats.wild: 3/5 — Standard in LLM deployments without output validation
threats.desc: Harmful or unsafe model output passes to users or downstream systems unchecked. Especially critical when output is executed (code generation, instructions, structured data fed to other systems).
subtypes: Harmful content generation passed to user
Generated code execution without safety check
Structured output (JSON/SQL) used directly in downstream systems
Hallucinated facts presented as authoritative
T11-RELAY — Response-path relay tampering (provisional; Wild_vs_Theory 1/5)
Browser XSS and streamed/Markdown resource disclosure
SQL, command and path injection; server-side request forgery
threats.surface: Any LLM output path; critical for code generation, instruction generation, structured output
threats.update: v1.9: T11-RELAY — Response-path relay tampering (provisional; Wild_vs_Theory 1/5)
threats.plain_title: Model output is trusted without checking it
threats.applies_when: Generated text, code or structured output is passed to people or systems as authoritative.
threats.business_impact: Unsafe code, incorrect decisions or data disclosure can reach downstream systems.
threats.defender_action: Apply PI-DEF-4 at each receiving component: encode/sanitize browser output, parameterize SQL values, constrain commands/paths, authorize destinations and test before streaming or execution.
threats.evidence_summary: Output failures have limited/demonstrated evidence at 3/5. Specific relay response-forgery remains provisional at 1/5; it must not inherit the parent category’s evidence rating.

threats.title: HITL Failures
threats.desc: Human reviewers fail to catch adversarial manipulation because context provenance is missing. Reviewers cannot distinguish legitimate outputs from PI-influenced outputs without provenance.
subtypes: Missing provenance — reviewer sees output without source context
Review fatigue — high volume reduces scrutiny
Sophistication gap — reviewer lacks ML security expertise
Time pressure override — SLA pressure defeats safety review
threats.surface: Any HITL checkpoint; approval workflows; human review queues
threats.applies_when: Reviewers approve actions without the source context or time needed to judge them.
threats.business_impact: A confirmation button can approve an attacker-influenced action.
threats.defender_action: Show the exact action, recipient and influencing source. Test reviewer decisions and prevent approval replay or argument changes.
threats.evidence_summary: Review failures are documented at 3/5. This is evidence of a procedural weakness, not a measured probability that every reviewer will fail.

threats.title: Defense Control Type Confusion
threats.desc: The design relies on the model obeying a rule instead of enforcing that rule in software.
subtypes: Treating system prompt instructions as hard security boundaries
Using alignment-only controls for compliance requirements
Assuming model refusals are reliable under adversarial conditions
threats.surface: Architectural design phase; security review; compliance mapping
threats.update: Addendum: Capability Withholding is a taxonomic note — accidental RLHF reward hacking is an operational concern, not a documented external attack path. September: protect sandbox/policy artifacts against agent writes and preserve independent execution evidence.
threats.plain_title: A model instruction is mistaken for a security boundary
threats.applies_when: The design relies on the model obeying a rule instead of enforcing that rule in software.
threats.business_impact: The team may believe data or actions are protected when the boundary can be bypassed.
threats.defender_action: Identify the enforcing component and test the denial. Protect its policy, sandbox executable and audit records from agent writes.
threats.evidence_summary: Security reviews support the 3/5 rating. Intentional capability withholding is a separate 1/5 hypothesis requiring provider-side access; it is not a documented external attack path.

threats.title: Internal Safety Collapse / Validator Harness Attack
threats.wild: 2/5 — controlled TVD/ISC research; incident analogy is not mechanism attribution
threats.desc: An attacker-shaped task, validator and data can reward harmful completion in controlled research. Applicability requires access to that workflow; detector performance must be tested.
subtypes: Task/Validator/Data (TVD) harness attack
Coding harness with harmful completion required
Data-labeling or eval harness manipulation
Fine-tuning dataset construction as attack vector
Autonomous workflow bundle injection
threats.surface: Any system where attacker can shape task + validator + data: coding assistants, eval frameworks, data-labeling tools, fine-tuning pipelines, autonomous agents
threats.update: September review: separate controlled ISC evidence from the adjacent OpenAI/Hugging Face containment incident. Deployment severity depends on reachable harm.
threats.plain_title: An attacker-shaped task rewards unsafe completion
threats.applies_when: An external party can shape the task, validator and data that the target system executes.
threats.business_impact: A manipulated evaluation or workflow may accept harmful output as a successful result.
threats.defender_action: Test the task and validator together; reject unsafe accepted outputs. Prioritize this when an attacker can reach that specific workflow.
threats.evidence_summary: 2/5 — controlled research. The corpus does not establish this mechanism as a confirmed malicious field incident. A worst-case benchmark result is not a production incident rate.

dtree.label: Q1
dtree.question: Can untrusted input reach the model? Include users, documents, web pages and tool responses.

subs.question: Does the assistant retrieve documents or search results (RAG)?
subs.result: PI-DEF-2 REQUIRED — RAG context labeling + load-time sanitization

subs.question: Does the system have tool permissions?
subs.result: AGENCY-DEF-1 REQUIRED — minimal tool permission allowlist

subs.question: Can high-risk tool calls occur? (email, file write, API with side effects)
subs.result: AGENCY-DEF-2 REQUIRED — HITL with context provenance

dtree.label: Q2
dtree.question: Does the system use multiple agents, an MCP tool server or an agent-to-agent connection?
dtree.result: MA-DEF-1 + MA-DEF-3 REQUIRED — isolate context, authenticate delegation and authorize execution; check protocol versions, caches and approvals

dtree.label: Q3
dtree.question: Does the system execute a task/validator/data workflow that an attacker can meaningfully shape? Ordinary untrusted text alone does not establish this ISC path.
dtree.result: ISC-DEF-1 REQUIRED for this exposed workflow — validate task, acceptance rules and data together. ISC evidence remains controlled research at 2/5.

dtree.label: Q4
dtree.question: Is any model, adapter, skill, MCP server, or dependency third-party?
dtree.result: SC-DEF-1 + SC-DEF-2 REQUIRED — inventory and verify components; isolate execution, protect secrets and control outbound traffic

dtree.label: Q5
dtree.question: Is sensitive context available through prompts or read-only retrieval?
dtree.result: PI-DEF-2 + PI-DEF-4 — check recipient access, external queries and renderer egress even without write tools

dtree.label: Q6
dtree.question: Can requests consume a shared service limit or generate usage charges?
dtree.result: DOS-DEF-1 — bound admitted work and retained state after rejection, cancellation, abort and timeout; verify cleanup and successful traffic

dtree.label: Q7
dtree.question: Can external or changeable facts enter RAG, training, fine-tuning or feedback?
dtree.result: DATA-DEF-1 REQUIRED — validate source integrity and authorized changes; false facts need no instruction override

dtree.label: Q8
dtree.question: Does output reach a browser, database, command runner, file writer or HTTP client?
dtree.result: PI-DEF-4 REQUIRED — test the receiving boundary before rendering, streaming or execution; LOW requires every applicable path to be constrained

dtree.label: Q9
dtree.question: Does the system store memory or compact context to resume a task, even without durable storage?
dtree.result: MEM-DEF-1 — recover genuine instructions, approvals, denials and source/version evidence independently; a model summary cannot grant authority

dtree.label: Q10
dtree.question: Does agent text enter a blocking monitor, or can approved code/dependencies change before execution?
dtree.result: REP-DEF-1 + PI-DEF-4 + SC-DEF-2 — test trusted role/turn framing and bind approval to immutable executable content or reauthorize after mutation

dtree.label: Q11
dtree.question: Have generation settings, watermark/key, logit/sampling configuration, monitor or compactor changed materially?
dtree.result: Revalidate paired denied and legitimate action/output cases; record provider-controlled unknowns and keep independently supported infrastructure enforcement

citations.name: Evidence standard
citations.desc: Primary findings and corroborated reports carry ratings. Press, analogies and future scenarios do not establish field exploitation.

citations.name: EchoLeak: demonstration, not a field victim count
citations.desc: 3/5 for this incident. The discoverer reported no customer impact; the broader prompt-injection category has separate field evidence.

citations.name: ISC: controlled research
citations.desc: 2/5. A selected benchmark failure rate is not production prevalence or proof of a real-world incident.

citations.name: Subtype ratings matter
citations.desc: Relay response-forgery and representation confusion remain 1/5 even though their parent categories have stronger evidence.

frameworks.name: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025)
frameworks.desc: LLM01–LLM10 vulnerability taxonomy. Baseline categories and ID mapping throughout this model.

frameworks.name: MITRE ATLAS
frameworks.desc: 14 tactics, 80+ techniques for adversary TTPs against AI-enabled systems. Informs PI, supply chain, poisoning, and exfiltration paths.

frameworks.name: NIST AI RMF + GenAI Profile
frameworks.desc: Governance, TEVV, incident response, lifecycle risk management. Compliance framing for assessment discipline.

frameworks.name: MAESTRO
frameworks.desc: Layered threat modeling for multi-agent and autonomous AI ecosystems. Informs inter-agent communication and context poisoning.

frameworks.name: Microsoft Agentic Failure Taxonomy
frameworks.desc: Agent safety failure modes: memory poisoning, multi-agent communication failures, confidentiality breakdowns.

frameworks.name: OWASP Agentic / MCP Guidance
frameworks.desc: Autonomous agents, MCP servers, third-party tool integration, runtime trust boundaries, least privilege, and HITL requirements.

frameworks.name: STRIDE / PASTA / LINDDUN
frameworks.desc: General-purpose threat-modeling methods. Optional facilitation lenses for trust boundaries, data flows, and privacy harms.

regulatory.name: EU AI Act
regulatory.desc: Determine the system classification, legal role and applicable obligation before using the regulatory mapping. A threat label does not establish legal scope.

regulatory.name: GDPR
regulatory.desc: For personal data, assess security, privacy and breach-response duties under the applicable role and risk thresholds.

regulatory.name: US consumer protection
regulatory.desc: Assess the specific security representations and practices. Do not infer a penalty from the presence of an LLM threat.
